text_changes.before:
The game is traversed automatically through a fixed sequence of commands extracted from the known walkthrough.
The Z-machine is
 deterministic:
 this sequence produces the same effects on every run.
The LLM is no longer 
responsible for 
advancing the story: it acts as a situated commentator, reading the situations in light of the available archives.
text_changes.after:
A fixed walkthrough advances the game; the model does not choose commands.
The current build uses Gemma 4 E4B for English commentary, with extended reasoning enabled.
Complete game outputs are buffered. The commentator notices a detail in the scene, using the interview as optional background.

text_changes.before:
The main material for this heritage mediation comes 
from a video 
interview with Amy Briggs by Jason Scott for the documentary
 Get 
Lamp.
I do not use this interview to explain the game linearly.
I place it in relation to the descriptions produced by 
Plundered Hearts 
through an embeddings-based
 mechanism,
 allowing semantic 
affinities to emerge 
(Bardiot, 2015).
text_changes.after:
Amy Briggs's interview with Jason Scott for Get Lamp supplies the documentary material.
Each of 25 interview clips is indexed by an embedding of its English subtitle transcript.
The generated comment is embedded in the same space. It becomes the bridge from the game to the archive; the game output itself is not vectorised.

text_changes.before:
At each step forward in the fiction, the LLM places the described situation in the context of
 Amy Briggs’s 
testimony.
The device gives rise to unexpected, sometimes obsessive 
connections between
 the heroine’s experience and the constraints of creating the game in 1987.
Each run produces a 
unique sequence,
 without claiming to produce original information.
text_changes.after:
The commentary is the semantic bridge between the game and Briggs's retrospective testimony.
Early prompts repeatedly returned to hardware limits, commercial pressure or genre. Reworking the prompt and its context reduced these patterns in the sampled readings.
A high similarity score can still yield a weak association. The sequence offers an interpretation; generated comments are not historical evidence.

text_changes.before:
The “knowledge base” is limited by Ministral-3:14B’s context capacity. A more comprehensive RAG needs to
 be
 implemented to compensate for training biases that may reproduce our social patterns.
The semantic proximity between the texts produced by the LLM and the transcript of Amy Briggs’s interview could be tested 
against different 
embedding models.
Improve intelligibility by 
translating
 the subtitles and using other video sources.
text_changes.after:
The new prompt reduces forced explanations, but can also weaken the explicit link to Briggs. Paraphrases, repetition and unsupported interpretations remain.
Cosine similarity ranks associations; it does not validate them. Recent-clip exclusions can also change which video is selected.
Next: assess game–comment–clip triples with human readers; compare shorter interview segments, embedding models and context positions.
